messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 66
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Roofer
- Trauma Type: Toxic chemical exposure
- Pcl5: 36

# The Weight of What He Breathed

Boon-Nam is a sixty-six-year-old Thai-born man who has spent the better part of four decades working rooftops across the Pacific Northwest. He is broad-shouldered and deliberate in the way he moves, a man who has always taken quiet pride in his physical reliability. He came to the United States in his late twenties, built a life with his wife Malee, raised two sons, and never once thought of himself as someone who would end up sitting in a therapist's office trying to explain why he can no longer sleep through the night.

Three years ago, Boon-Nam was part of a crew hired to remove and replace the roofing on a large commercial warehouse. Midway through the second day, something went wrong with a ventilation system below. A chemical mixture — later identified as containing industrial solvents and a byproduct of a manufacturing process stored in the building — vented directly upward through gaps in the old roofing material. Boon-Nam describes the moment with a kind of careful flatness, as though he is trying to hold the memory at arm's length: a smell like burning plastic and something sweet underneath it, a burning in his throat, his eyes going wrong, his legs giving out before he understood what was happening. Two of his crew members collapsed beside him. He remembers lying on the roof, unable to call out, watching the sky tilt.

He was hospitalized for four days. The physical recovery, doctors told him, was good. But Boon-Nam does not feel recovered.

In the months that followed, he returned to work — or tried to. Standing on a roof, he finds himself scanning constantly, sniffing the air, his body coiled in a way that exhausts him by midday. Any chemical smell, even something as ordinary as a neighbor's cleaning products drifting through an open window, sends a cold wave through his chest and pulls him back to that tilting sky. He has learned to leave rooms quietly rather than explain himself. His crew has noticed that he works more slowly now, that he sometimes stops and stares at nothing.

At home, Malee has become the quiet keeper of what he will not say. She knows not to use certain cleaning sprays. She knows that Thursdays — the day of the week it happened — are harder. Boon-Nam does not tell her about the dreams, which come several times a week and always end the same way: with him unable to move, unable to speak, watching something approach that he cannot name. He wakes with his heart hammering and lies still in the dark, not wanting to disturb her, not wanting to be the kind of man who needs comforting at three in the morning.

He is irritable in ways that shame him. He snapped at his younger son last month over something trivial and saw the surprise on his son's face — the careful, cautious look — and recognized it as fear. That look has stayed with him.

Boon-Nam does not think of himself as traumatized. He thinks of himself as someone who breathed something he should not have breathed and who has not yet gotten back to himself. He talks about his body as a machine that is running slightly off, a roof that is not quite sealed. It is the language he trusts. He scores a thirty-six on the PCL-5, though the numbers mean little to him. What means something is that he used to love the height, the open air, the particular satisfaction of a finished ridge line. He is not sure he loves it anymore. He is not sure what he loves, and that uncertainty, more than the nightmares or the flinching or the sleeplessness, is what finally brought him here — the slow, disorienting realization that the man he was before that afternoon on the roof has not entirely come back down.
